Entities, Relationships, Cardinality &
Ownership
Turn product language into relational structure

Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling

Architecture milestone

Production-ready relational model

↓

Persistent TaskFlow CRUD

Phase 10 decides what the durable data should mean before Phase 11 writes application behavior against it.

Start with business language, not tables
A common modeling mistake is to begin by inventing table names. Start instead with statements the business expects to
remain true. Example: a workspace has many projects; a project belongs to exactly one workspace; a task belongs to
one project; a workspace has many members; a user can belong to many workspaces.

Figure 1 - Business rules become relationships

Business statement

↓

Cardinality

↓

Foreign key / join model

↓

Database invariant

The schema is a durable encoding of business relationships, not a mirror of one screen.

Entity candidates
Candidate                 Why it exists                                       Not just a field because...

User                      Identity referenced across workspaces               It has its own lifecycle and relationships

Workspace                 Collaboration/security boundary                     Many projects and memberships depend on it

Membership                User-to-workspace participation                     It has role/status metadata

Project                   Groups tasks inside a workspace                     It has ownership, dates and task relationships

Task                      Work item tracked by the system                     It has state, priority and relationships

Cardinality
Relationship                        Meaning                                                     Relational shape

Workspace 1 -> many Projects        Each project belongs to one workspace                       projects.workspace_id FK

Project 1 -> many Tasks             Each task belongs to one project                            tasks.project_id FK

User many <-> many Workspace        Users join many workspaces and vice versa                   memberships join table

Optionality is part of cardinality
"A task may have an assignee" is different from "every task must have an assignee." The first permits a NULL assignee
reference. The second should be NOT NULL. Optionality should follow domain rules, not convenience.

Ownership vs association

A task can be associated with an assignee without the assignee owning the containing project. Ownership affects
security and lifecycle decisions. Model this distinction explicitly rather than assuming every foreign key means
ownership.
A useful review question: If the parent disappears, should the child disappear too? If the answer is unclear, you have not
finished modeling lifecycle ownership.

Exercise
For each statement below, identify entity candidates, cardinality, optionality, and the likely foreign key or join entity: (1)
projects may have an optional due date, (2) users can join many workspaces, (3) each project belongs to one
workspace, (4) a task can optionally be assigned to one workspace member.

Optionality, Keys & Constraints
Put invariants in the database instead of only in application code

Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling
Volume 03 - Database Engineering

Architecture milestone

PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure

↓

Production-ready relational model

↓

Persistent TaskFlow CRUD

Phase 10 decides what the durable data should mean before Phase 11 writes application behavior against it.

A valid row is more than a TypeScript object
Database constraints remain active regardless of which application code writes the row. They are therefore the final line
of defense for structural integrity.

Figure 1 - Integrity layers

UI validation

↓

API validation

↓

Business rules

↓

Database constraints

The closer a rule is to a permanent data invariant, the stronger the case for enforcing it in the database too.

Primary keys
Every durable entity needs a stable identity. For TaskFlow, UUID-style IDs are appropriate for entities that may cross
service/API boundaries. The course will use UUID-compatible Prisma String IDs generated with uuid() for production
entities.

Natural vs surrogate keys
Key type                    Example                              Trade-off

Natural                     email address                        Readable but business values can change

Surrogate                   generated UUID                       Stable identity independent of business attributes

Uniqueness
Uniqueness should reflect business invariants. Example: a workspace slug may be globally unique; a membership
should be unique for the pair (workspaceId, userId); project names may or may not be unique depending on product
rules.
@@unique([workspaceId, userId])

NULL is a domain decision
Field                             Possible rule                                              Schema implication

Project.name                      Always required                                            NOT NULL

Task.description                  Optional narrative                                         nullable

Task.assigneeId                   Unassigned is allowed                                      nullable FK

Field                             Possible rule                                    Schema implication

Task.completedAt                  Only present when completed                      nullable timestamp

Check-like invariants
Prisma schema syntax does not express every possible PostgreSQL CHECK constraint directly. When the database
must guarantee an invariant that exceeds ORM-level expressiveness, use reviewed SQL migrations rather than
pretending the invariant does not exist.
Do not encode every business rule as a database constraint. Workflow rules that require external state, permissions, or
multiple aggregates usually belong in application services. Use the database for structural invariants it can enforce reliably.

Exercise
Classify each rule as primarily database constraint, service rule, or both: unique workspace slug; user must be
workspace member before task assignment; task title required; invoice approval requires manager role; membership
pair must be unique.

Many-to-Many Membership & Composite
Uniqueness
Model collaboration as a first-class relationship

Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling
Volume 03 - Database Engineering

Architecture milestone

PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure

↓

Production-ready relational model

↓

Persistent TaskFlow CRUD

Phase 10 decides what the durable data should mean before Phase 11 writes application behavior against it.

Why a bare many-to-many is not enough
Users and workspaces are many-to-many, but their relationship has meaningful data: role, status, joinedAt, and possibly
invitation metadata. That means the relationship deserves its own entity: Membership.

Figure 1 - Explicit join entity

User

↓

Membership
role / status / joinedAt

↓

Workspace

Membership is not plumbing. It is a domain record with its own behavior and constraints.

Core invariant
A user should normally have at most one active membership record per workspace. Encode the structural uniqueness
with a composite unique constraint.
model Membership {
id          String   @id @default(uuid())
userId      String
workspaceId String
role        MembershipRole @default(MEMBER)
joinedAt    DateTime @default(now())

user           User      @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id])
workspace      Workspace @relation(fields: [workspaceId], references: [id])

@@unique([workspaceId, userId])
@@index([userId])
}

Why both an id and composite uniqueness?
The surrogate id gives the membership a stable independent identity for APIs/audit events. The composite uniqueness
protects the relationship invariant. They solve different problems.

Role belongs on membership
A user can be ADMIN in Workspace A and MEMBER in Workspace B. Therefore role cannot be modeled as one global
User.role if role is workspace-scoped.
This is a foundational enterprise pattern: identity is global, permissions are often contextual. HRIS department
membership, tenant membership, project membership and organization membership all use similar relational reasoning.

Assignment should target membership or user?
For TaskFlow, a task assignee ultimately represents a user participating in the workspace. Modeling assignee as userId
is simpler, but then service logic must verify workspace membership. Modeling assigneeMembershipId makes
membership validity structural but couples task assignment to membership row lifecycle. The course will use assigneeId
-> User for clarity and enforce membership in the service layer later.

Enums, Lookup Tables & State Modeling
Choose the right representation for finite business states

Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling
Volume 03 - Database Engineering

Architecture milestone

PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure

↓

Production-ready relational model

↓

Persistent TaskFlow CRUD

Phase 10 decides what the durable data should mean before Phase 11 writes application behavior against it.

Not every string should be free text
Values such as task status and priority usually come from a constrained set. Free-text values create invalid states such
as "INPROGRESS", "in_progress", and "Doing" describing the same concept.

Three common options
Approach                        Good for                                     Cost

Application string              Prototype-only values                        Weak integrity

Database/Prisma enum            Small stable finite set                      Schema migration to change values

Lookup table                    Admin-configurable or metadata-rich set      More joins and lifecycle complexity

TaskFlow choice
enum TaskStatus {
TODO
IN_PROGRESS
DONE
CANCELED
}

enum TaskPriority {
LOW
MEDIUM
HIGH
URGENT
}

enum MembershipRole {
OWNER
ADMIN
MEMBER
}

Why enums here?
These values are small, have clear semantics, and are expected to change infrequently. They are part of the application
contract and are good candidates for enums.

When a lookup table would be better
If each status needs configurable color, ordering, SLA behavior, translations, or customer-defined values, it has become
data rather than a fixed code-level state. A lookup table may then be more appropriate.
Do not use enums for values likely to be customized per tenant. Schema migrations are a poor substitute for normal
application data management.

State transitions are not automatically database constraints
An enum can guarantee that status is one of the allowed values, but it does not guarantee valid transitions such as
TODO -> DONE. Transition permissions and workflow rules belong in the service layer unless a database trigger is
intentionally part of the architecture.

lessons.body:
Deletion, Referential Actions & Lifecycle
Design what happens when related data disappears

Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling
Volume 03 - Database Engineering

Architecture milestone

PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure

↓

Production-ready relational model

↓

Persistent TaskFlow CRUD

Phase 10 decides what the durable data should mean before Phase 11 writes application behavior against it.

Delete is a business operation
A foreign key answers whether related rows may exist. A referential action answers what the database should do when
the referenced row is updated or deleted. This should follow ownership and retention requirements.

Action                       Meaning                                                 Typical use

Cascade                      Delete children automatically                           Strong ownership, e.g. project-local tasks

Restrict / NoAction          Block parent deletion                                   Records must be handled deliberately

SetNull                      Keep child, clear optional reference                    Optional assignee/reference

Application-managed          Service performs explicit archival/deletion workflow    Audited enterprise processes

TaskFlow lifecycle choices
Relationship                           Suggested behavior                 Reason

Workspace -> Project                   Cascade in learning model          Projects have no meaning outside workspace

Project -> Task                        Cascade                            Tasks belong to project

User -> Membership                     Cascade/explicit cleanup dependingMembership
audit needs depends on user identity

User -> Task assignee                  SetNull                            Task should survive account removal

Workspace -> Membership                Cascade                            Membership is scoped to workspace

workspace Workspace @relation(fields: [workspaceId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
assignee User?      @relation(fields: [assigneeId], references: [id], onDelete: SetNull)

Soft deletion is not free
Adding deletedAt looks simple but changes almost every query, uniqueness rule, reporting workflow, restore behavior
and index strategy. Do not add soft deletion merely because enterprise systems often use it.
Production retention requirements may require archival instead of cascading hard deletes. The course model teaches
relational ownership, but a regulated HRIS or accounting system should derive lifecycle from explicit retention policy.

Exercise
Choose and justify an on-delete behavior for comments, file attachments, activity log rows, and workspace invitations.
There is no universally correct answer; the point is to connect lifecycle semantics to referential actions.

Indexes & Query-Driven Design
Design access paths from real application queries

Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling
Volume 03 - Database Engineering

Architecture milestone

PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure

↓

Production-ready relational model

↓

Persistent TaskFlow CRUD

Phase 10 decides what the durable data should mean before Phase 11 writes application behavior against it.

Do not index every column
Indexes trade storage and write cost for faster access paths. Index design should start from important query patterns,
not from a desire to "optimize" every field.

Figure 1 - Query-driven indexing

Product requirement

↓

Frequent query

↓

Filter / join / sort columns

↓

Candidate index

↓

Measure with real workload

Indexes are consequences of access patterns.

Expected TaskFlow queries
Query                                                 Likely columns

List projects in workspace                            workspaceId + createdAt/name

List tasks in project                                 projectId + status + createdAt

My assigned tasks                                     assigneeId + status

Find memberships for user                             userId

Resolve workspace by slug                             slug unique

Candidate Prisma indexes
model Task {
// ...
@@index([projectId, status])
@@index([assigneeId, status])
@@index([createdAt])
}

model Project {
// ...
@@index([workspaceId])
}

Composite index order matters
An index on (projectId, status) is naturally useful for queries beginning with projectId. It is not equivalent to (status,
projectId) for every workload. The order should reflect leading filter/selectivity and sort patterns.

Foreign keys are not automatically all the indexes you need
A foreign-key constraint protects referential integrity. Query performance is a separate concern. PostgreSQL does not
automatically create an index on the referencing foreign-key column simply because the foreign key exists.
Performance design rule: model correctness first, then choose indexes from observed high-value queries, and validate with
EXPLAIN/production-like data later.

Normalization & Denormalization
Avoid duplicated truth without turning the schema into theory theater

Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling
Volume 03 - Database Engineering

Architecture milestone

PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure

↓

Production-ready relational model

↓

Persistent TaskFlow CRUD

Phase 10 decides what the durable data should mean before Phase 11 writes application behavior against it.

What normalization is trying to prevent
Normalization reduces contradictory copies of the same fact. If workspace name is repeated on every task, renaming
the workspace requires changing many rows and creates opportunities for inconsistency.

Figure 1 - One source of truth

Task rows repeat workspaceName

↓

Update anomaly

↓

Normalize Workspace

↓

Tasks reference workspace indirectly through Project

Relationships replace duplicated facts with references to authoritative records.

Practical normal form mindset
Question                                                     Healthy direction

Does each row represent one thing?                           Yes - avoid repeating groups

Does an attribute depend on the whole identity?              Yes - avoid partial dependencies

Is a fact stored in the entity that owns it?                 Yes - avoid transitive duplication

Do not over-normalize labels into pointless tables
A three-value stable priority does not automatically need a task_priorities table. Normalization is about dependency and
truth, not maximizing table count.

When denormalization can be intentional
Read-heavy reporting, immutable historical snapshots, analytics, search documents, or expensive aggregate views can
justify duplicated derived data. But denormalization should name the consistency strategy explicitly.
Never duplicate a field because JOINs "feel slow" without measurement. Relational databases are designed to join
normalized data efficiently when keys and indexes are appropriate.

TaskFlow examples
•
Workspace name belongs on Workspace, not Task.
•
Membership role belongs on Membership, not globally on User.
•
Task status belongs on Task because it is a fact about that task.

•
A future immutable audit event may snapshot labels because history should not change when the live record
changes.

The model we are committing to
Figure 1 - TaskFlow production relational model

User

↓

Membership

↓

Workspace

↓

Project

↓

Task

The visual is simplified: Membership connects User <-> Workspace; Workspace owns Projects; Project owns Tasks; Task may reference
an assignee User.

Model overview
Model                       Core responsibility

User                        Application identity/profile reference

Workspace                   Tenant/collaboration boundary

Membership                  User participation and workspace-scoped role

Project                     Container of related work inside workspace

Task                        Work item inside project

Prisma schema snapshot
enum MembershipRole {
OWNER
ADMIN
MEMBER
}

enum TaskStatus {
TODO
IN_PROGRESS
DONE
CANCELED
}

enum TaskPriority {
LOW

MEDIUM
HIGH
URGENT
}

model User {
id          String                @id @default(uuid())
email       String                @unique
displayName String?
createdAt   DateTime              @default(now())
updatedAt   DateTime              @updatedAt

memberships Membership[]
assignedTasks Task[]     @relation("TaskAssignee")
}

model Workspace {
id          String                @id @default(uuid())
name        String
slug        String                @unique
createdAt   DateTime              @default(now())
updatedAt   DateTime              @updatedAt

memberships Membership[]
projects    Project[]
}

model Membership {
id          String         @id @default(uuid())
userId      String
workspaceId String
role        MembershipRole @default(MEMBER)
joinedAt    DateTime       @default(now())

user           User      @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
workspace      Workspace @relation(fields: [workspaceId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)

@@unique([workspaceId, userId])
@@index([userId])
}

model Project {
id          String            @id @default(uuid())
workspaceId String
name        String
description String?
createdAt   DateTime          @default(now())
updatedAt   DateTime          @updatedAt

workspace      Workspace @relation(fields: [workspaceId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
tasks          Task[]

@@index([workspaceId])
}

model Task {
id          String       @id @default(uuid())
projectId   String
assigneeId String?
title       String
description String?
status      TaskStatus   @default(TODO)
priority    TaskPriority @default(MEDIUM)
dueAt       DateTime?
completedAt DateTime?
createdAt   DateTime     @default(now())
updatedAt   DateTime     @updatedAt

project        Project @relation(fields: [projectId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)
assignee       User?   @relation("TaskAssignee", fields: [assigneeId], references: [id], onDelete: SetNull)

@@index([projectId, status])

@@index([assigneeId, status])
}

Important service-layer invariant
The schema can prove that assigneeId references a real User, but it does not prove that the user belongs to the task
project's workspace. Later Todos/Tasks service logic must verify workspace membership before assignment. This is a
perfect example of database integrity plus application business rules working together.

Why User exists before Supabase Auth integration
Supabase Auth identity will arrive later. TaskFlow still benefits from an application-facing User/Profile model that can
participate in relational data. Phase 17 will define how authenticated identity maps to this model without trusting
browser-supplied user IDs.
The production model is intentionally capable but not maximal. Comments, attachments, activity events, labels, invitations,
notifications and audit logs will be added only when later product phases create concrete requirements.

Migration Planning & Safe Schema
Evolution
Change durable data without treating migrations as generated noise

Phase 10 - Relational Data Modeling
Volume 03 - Database Engineering

Architecture milestone

PostgreSQL + Prisma infrastructure

↓

Production-ready relational model

↓

Persistent TaskFlow CRUD

Phase 10 decides what the durable data should mean before Phase 11 writes application behavior against it.

A schema change is a data change
Once production data exists, changing schema can affect stored rows, constraints, application compatibility, indexes,
lock duration, and rollback strategy. Migrations deserve code review.

Figure 1 - Safe change workflow

Change business requirement

↓

Edit schema

↓

Generate migration

↓

Review SQL

↓

Backfill / stage if needed

↓

Apply + verify

The migration file is part of the application codebase and deployment story.

Additive changes are easiest
Adding a nullable column is usually easier than immediately adding a required column to a populated table. For required
new data, use a staged migration: add nullable/default, backfill, validate, then enforce NOT NULL.

Example staged change
Step                Action

1                   Add optional workspace timezone

2                   Deploy code that can write it

3                   Backfill existing workspaces

4                   Add required constraint if product truly requires it

5                   Remove temporary compatibility code

Renames can be destructive if generated naively

An ORM may interpret a field rename as drop-old + add-new, which can lose data. Review generated SQL and use
deliberate SQL rename operations or migration edits when preserving existing data matters.

Environment workflow
Environment                               Command intent

Development                               migrate dev creates/tests migration

CI / staging / production                 migrate deploy applies committed migrations

Never production                          ad-hoc migrate dev against live data

A rollback is not automatically "run the migration backward." Many database changes are irreversible after data is
transformed or deleted. Production change planning should prefer forward fixes, backups, compatibility windows, and explicit
restore strategy.

Phase 10 migration plan
•
Replace the minimal Todo-only learning model with the TaskFlow production model in a controlled development
migration.
•
Review generated SQL before applying.
•
Use a development database/shadow workflow only.
•
Verify tables, foreign keys, uniqueness and indexes after migration.
•
Do not seed production-like identities until authentication design is introduced.

Level 1 - Follow
Recreate the TaskFlow production model on paper or in a diagram. For every foreign key, write the sentence it
represents. Example: Project.workspaceId means every project belongs to one existing workspace.

Level 2 - Modify
Add an optional Project.dueAt and decide whether it needs an index. Explain your decision from query patterns rather
than intuition.

Level 3 - Implement
Design a Comment model for tasks. Decide its author relationship, deletion behavior, timestamps, and indexes. Do not
copy a generic schema; justify each choice.

Level 4 - Engineer
Design workspace invitations without writing application code. Requirements: invite by email, invitation expires,
accepting creates membership, repeated active invitations should be controlled, history may need to remain after
acceptance. Produce entities, constraints, indexes, and lifecycle policy.

Architecture oral exam
Question                                          Expected reasoning

Why is Membership an entity?                      Many-to-many relationship carries role/status/time metadata

Why role is not User.role?                        Role is workspace-scoped

Why assigneeId can be nullable?                   Unassigned task is valid

Why FK does not prove membership?                 FK proves user exists, not contextual workspace membership

Why composite unique membership?                  Prevents duplicate user-workspace relationship

Why not index every field?                        Indexes cost storage and write maintenance

•
I can distinguish entity, attribute and relationship.
•
I can identify 1:1, 1:many and many:many relationships.
•
I can justify NULL vs NOT NULL.
•
I can identify database invariants vs service-layer business rules.
•
I can design a join entity when a relationship has data.
•
I understand composite uniqueness.
•
I can choose cascade/restrict/set-null intentionally.
•
I can propose indexes from query patterns.
•
I understand normalization as one-source-of-truth reasoning.
•
I can review a schema change as a migration/data operation.
•
I can explain the complete TaskFlow relational model without reading the code.

Phase 10 is complete when you can explain not only what tables exist, but why each relationship, constraint,
optional field, index, and lifecycle decision exists. Phase 11 will then implement persistent CRUD against this model.

Debugging Workshop — Phase 10: Relational Data Modeling

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
Business nouns -> entities -> relationships/cardinality -> constraints -> Prisma models -> migration -> seeded graph

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — JSON arrays replacing relational join tables without reason
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Debugging exit ticket

lessons.body:
Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Relational Data Modeling

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 10 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Translate TaskFlow business relationships into a relational model that can enforce membership, ordering, labels, comments, ownership, and lifecycle rules.

Required artifact
A complete Prisma/ER model for TaskFlow core entities with keys, relation tables, uniqueness, and important indexes.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can explain every cardinality.
• Can justify join tables.
• Can identify invariants enforced by constraints.
• Can query the model from parent and child directions.

Independent build sequence
1. List TaskFlow nouns and separate entities from attributes and events.
2. Model workspace membership as an explicit relation carrying role/state rather than an array on User.
3. Model boards/lists/tasks and decide which parent IDs should be required.
4. Model labels through a join table and explain composite uniqueness.
5. Add comments and timestamps with intentional delete behavior.
6. Seed a small realistic graph and query it from several directions to validate the model.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 10: Relational Data Modeling. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact
A complete Prisma/ER model for TaskFlow core entities with keys, relation tables, uniqueness, and important indexes.

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.

TaskFlow Phase 10 relational model reference

This snapshot is the teaching model used at the end of Phase 10.
It is not a complete final enterprise schema. Later phases add features only when their requirements become concrete.

Important service invariant:
- Task.assigneeId references User. Service logic must verify that the assignee is a member of the task project's workspace.

Prisma remains locked to 7.9.1 for this course.

# Relational modeling checklist

- What durable business fact does this model represent?
- What is its stable identity?
- Which fields are required vs optional?
- Which values must be unique?
- What relationships exist and what is their cardinality?
- Does the relationship carry its own metadata?
- What happens when each parent is deleted?
- Which invariants belong in database constraints?
- Which rules require application/service context?
- What high-value queries will need indexes?
- Is any fact duplicated unnecessarily?
- How will this schema evolve after data exists?
